criterion_notes.c1: Examines household-level sanitation service access, specifically connection versus non-connection (and misconnection to storm/surface drains) to the Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA) foul-water sewer network in urban Dhaka.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading: Yes — directly examines administrative, institutional, financial/tariff, and legal/regulatory barriers to sewer connection alongside psychosocial determinants. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline due to RANAS behavioural framing, but passes on primary empirical rule-type mechanisms). Although the paper structures its intervention recommendations around the psychological RANAS framework and Behaviour Change Techniques (BCTs), its primary quantitative survey (N = 384) and qualitative IDIs/FGDs directly measure and analyse concrete rule-type mechanisms governing sewer access: (1) administrative burden in DWASA connection and maintenance application procedures (complicated administrative processes, bureaucratic delays, lack of procedural guidance, written applications and office visits to DWASA ignored, and procedural knowledge/confidence), (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (high upfront DWASA connection fees relative to city corporation drains and mandatory monthly DWASA sewer billing imposed even on unconnected households in sewered zones, Table 1 p = 0.0002 and qualitative findings), (3) municipal approval and legal barriers ('No approval from city corporation' in Table 2 and 'Legal issues' obstructing connection in Table 3; non-significance does not affect eligibility per A18), and (4) utility/municipal institutional structure (jurisdictional responsibility-shifting between DWASA and the city corporation).
criterion_notes.c3: Primary mixed-methods empirical study conducted between October 2023 and November 2024 combining a stratified survey of 384 household/building owners (192 connected, 192 not-connected) with 10 in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports verified household connection status to the DWASA foul-water sewer network (connected vs. not-connected / misconnected to open or city corporation drains) as well as household satisfaction with wastewater service access.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (building/household owners in 10 Dhaka neighbourhoods across 5 DWASA MODS zones, N = 384 survey respondents plus 10 IDIs and 2 FGDs), exposures (RANAS psychosocial factors alongside administrative connection burden, DWASA sewer billing and connection-fee rules, city corporation approval/legal issues, and institutional fragmentation), outcome (confirmed DWASA sewer connection vs. non-connection), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods comparative study).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This mixed-method cross-sectional study aimed to develop targeted, evidence-based interventions to increase sewer connections in urban communities. We surveyed 384 households and conducted 10 in-depth interviews and two focus group discussions across five DWASA zones.

In order to ensure equitable representation of households with DWASA sewer connections and those with city corporations or open drainage, 384 households were enrolled through stratified matching, the details were described in earlier research (Alam et al., 2025). During visits, trained enumerators confirmed the type of connection in each household.

Qualitative findings revealed widespread dissatisfaction with dysfunctional drainage systems, high connection costs, inadequate maintenance support from DWASA, and bureaucratic delays as significant barriers. These results highlight a complex interplay of psychological, financial, and administrative challenges limiting sewer uptake.

We wrote to them (DWASA). We gave them applications requesting maintenance. We went to their offices for support. However, they just told us it was not solely their responsibility (indicating the involvement of the city corporation).

DWASA bill is already burdening us, but we are not getting any service. I am connected to city corporation’s drain. And the cost of connecting new households to the sewer is also higher than connecting to city corporation drain. That fee should be reduced also
Respondents were split equally into connected to sewer (n = 192) and not-connected to sewer (n = 192).

raw_response.exposure: Administrative connection procedures and bureaucratic delays, DWASA tariff/billing and new-connection fee rules (including monthly sewer billing of unconnected households and high upfront connection fees), city corporation approval and legal barriers, institutional responsibility division between DWASA and the city corporation, and RANAS psychosocial determinants
raw_response.outcome: Household connection to the DWASA foul-water sewer network versus non-connection (use of city corporation or open drainage / sewer misconnection) and satisfaction with current wastewater access
raw_response.population_and_sample: Household/building owners (landlords) across 10 neighbourhoods in five DWASA Maintenance, Operation, Distribution, and Services (MODS) zones in Dhaka, Bangladesh: 384 surveyed households (192 connected to DWASA sewer, 192 not-connected to sewer) plus 10 in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions (6-10 male participants each) with unconnected landlords
raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods cross-sectional study in Dhaka, Bangladesh satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2. Although its intervention design uses the psychosocial RANAS framework and Behaviour Change Techniques, the primary empirical investigation (N = 384 stratified household survey plus 10 IDIs and 2 FGDs with landlords) directly examines concrete rule-type mechanisms governing household sewer connection: administrative burden and bureaucratic delays in DWASA connection/maintenance application procedures, utility tariff and cost-recovery rules (mandatory monthly DWASA sewer billing of unconnected households alongside high upfront connection fees), municipal approval and legal issues (Tables 2 and 3), and institutional responsibility-shifting between DWASA and the city corporation. Per the protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal/administrative evidence and statistically non-significant quantitative comparisons (e.g., legal issues and city corporation approval) remain eligible.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods comparative study (stratified household survey, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussions)
